title: Car USB charger: safe teardown
summary: A working car USB charger is a ready-made 12 V to USB converter: keep it whole. A dead one gives very little and is rarely worth the time: a USB socket or two, a small inductor, a few low-voltage capacitors, some springs and sometimes a fuse. It runs on 12 V (some on 24 V too), so the shock risk is low, but a shorted car battery can start a fire, and the plastic shell can crack and fly when you open it.

steps.text: Test it whole first. Plug it into a working 12 V socket, or feed it from a bench supply set to 12 V with the current limit turned down (about 1 A for each USB-A port you will load), or from a 12 V battery through a fused lead with the fuse left out until the leads are on (skill_dc_wiring). The tip is positive and the side springs negative. Measure DC volts between the two outer pins of a USB-A socket: you want about 5 V. A USB-C port reads nothing until a phone is plugged in, so test that port by charging a phone. Read the label for the input range (the Belkin teardown gives DC 12 V, the Ugreen teardown 12–24 V) and never feed it more than that.
steps.warn: Check polarity with the meter before you connect any lead. Fuse the positive lead within 30 cm of the battery, at 1–1.5 A for each port. A short across a car battery melts wire and starts fires. If the charger gets warm, smells or smokes, disconnect it and scrap it.

steps.text: If it works, stop here. A working car charger is worth far more whole than in parts: it is a ready-made 12 V to USB converter for a battery or solar charging point (build_usb_charging_station).
Unplug it from the socket, battery lead or bench supply and let it cool if it was hot. Work over a tray: the tip, spring and side contacts are small and loose once the case opens.

If there is a metal ring at the tip, unscrew it and catch the tip contact and its spring. Look for a fuse behind them (iFixit's troubleshooting guide unscrews the tip to reach a 2.5 A fuse); some have only the spring (iFixit generic charger).
Look for screws under labels and stickers and take them out.

No screws: find the cap round the USB ports or the seam along the body, and work a plastic opening tool or old card into it, a little at a time. If no seam opens, iFixit got the PureGear's shell apart by squeezing it with locking pliers until its tabs let go: cloth over the jaws, go gently, and hold the shell, never the board. A welded shell (the Belkin's is ultrasonically welded) may not give, so leave it whole.
steps.warn: Wear safety glasses: the shell can crack and throw pieces. If you must use a blade, clamp the charger first and never hold it in your free hand.

steps.text: Slide the board out. Note which contact goes where: the tip spring is positive, the side springs negative. Photograph it before anything falls out.

To reuse the board as a 12 V to 5 V converter, solder a red wire to the tip contact's pad and a black wire to a side contact's pad. Check the label's input range and feed the board no more than that. Check polarity with the meter before you connect the battery. Fuse the red wire within 30 cm of the battery (skill_dc_wiring), and test the output with the meter before you plug in a phone.
To strip a dead board, unsolder the USB sockets, the inductor, the electrolytic capacitors and the LED. Write each capacitor's voltage and value on its bag.
steps.warn: Soldering irons and fresh joints burn. Work on a heat-proof surface and park the iron in its stand.

steps.text: Bag the parts from each charger together with a note of its label rating. Throw away the shell and any small surface-mount chips.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

Be honest with yourself: a working car charger is the prize. A dead one gives a few small parts: iFixit's generic charger board held only two capacitors, an inductor, a diode, an LED and a USB port (iFixit generic charger), and the chips on newer boards are too small to reuse by hand. Open a dead one only if you need those few parts.

- **The whole charger, working.** It turns 12 V from a car, a battery or a solar system into USB power and handles the phone's charging handshake. Fit several to a fused 12 V bus for a charging station (build_usb_charging_station).
- **The board, as a converter.** The buck (step-down) circuit inside works from bare wires. The Belkin F8J251 uses two CX8850 step-down controllers rated for up to 40 V input; the Ugreen CD213 uses an SC8112 converter (Chongdiantou Belkin; Chongdiantou Ugreen). Feed only what the label allows.
- **USB sockets.** For a home-made 5 V outlet.
- **Inductor.** A small power inductor: spares for other small converters.
- **Electrolytic capacitors.** Low-voltage parts, such as 35 V 10 µF at the input and 16 V 470 µF and 6.3 V 330 µF at the outputs of the Belkin (Chongdiantou Belkin), and 35 V 100 µF in and 16 V 220 µF out on each Ugreen board (Chongdiantou Ugreen). Reuse only at or below their marked voltage.
- **Fuse.** Some have one, some don't (see Variations). iFixit's troubleshooting guide for a generic 1 A charger unscrews the tip to reach a 2.5 A, 125 V fuse, while its teardown of a generic 1 A charger found only a spring and no fuse (iFixit generic troubleshooting; iFixit generic charger). A fuse you find is a spare: check it with the meter on continuity.
- **Springs and contacts.** Small springs and metal contacts for battery holders and test leads.
- **LED.** A status light.

## How they work, and what that means for reuse

- A cheap charger may use an MC34063 regulator. From the parts in its generic 1 A unit, iFixit worked out a maximum output of about 0.68 A, short of the label's 1 A (iFixit generic charger). That was a calculation, not a measurement, and one unit, so a label on a cheap charger may not be true.
- USB-C chargers carry a power delivery chip that agrees a higher voltage, such as 9 V or 12 V, with the phone. The Ugreen's ports are rated 5 V 3 A, 9 V 2.22 A or 12 V 1.67 A (Chongdiantou Ugreen). A USB-C source puts no voltage on the port until a device is attached (TI TPS65982), so a bare meter reads 0 V there.
- Input range matters: the Belkin teardown gives its input as DC 12 V and the Ugreen teardown gives 12–24 V (Chongdiantou Belkin; Chongdiantou Ugreen). The 40 V limit is the Belkin chip's rating, not the charger's. Check the label before using one on a 24 V truck or battery bank.

## Variations

- **Generic 1 A charger:** two small screws, one hidden under the label; a metal end cap that pries off; a screw-on tip ring with only a spring behind it and no fuse; an MC34063 regulator, two capacitors, an inductor, a diode and an LED, with no other protection (iFixit generic charger).
- **PureGear Extreme (12 W):** no screws; the lid pried off with a plastic tool and the shell came apart when squeezed across the seam with locking pliers. Inside: an ACT4533C step-down converter, a USB charging interface chip, an inductor, two diodes and a fuse on the board (iFixit PureGear).
- **Belkin F8J251 (30 W, USB-A and USB-C):** the shell is ultrasonically welded; the positive input is a spring with a metal plate on its tail; two step-down circuits, one per port (Chongdiantou Belkin).
- **Ugreen CD213 (40 W, two USB-C):** the top cover is held by clips and the module comes out of an aluminium shell, insulated from it by paper. Two identical boards, each with its own converter, power delivery chip and output switch, and a surface-mount fuse (Chongdiantou Ugreen).
- **Other 12 V plugs:** a Slime portable air compressor's plug has a 15 A fuse that you reach by unscrewing the tip (iFixit Slime); other 12 V plugs may too.

## What to leave

- Welded shells, unless you really want the parts.
- Surface-mount chips: too small to reuse by hand.
- Chargers that ran hot or smell burnt.

## Testing what you got out

- **Board:** feed 12 V through a fuse with nothing plugged in and measure the output; then add a load, such as a phone or a small 5 V lamp, and check it holds about 5 V and stays cool.
- **Fuse:** near 0 Ω is good; open means blown (test_continuity).
- **Capacitors:** see test_capacitor.
